data.text:
Time‐varying measures of cerebral network centrality correlate with visual saliency during movie watching
DOI: 10.1002/brb3.2334
Brain and Behavior (Wiley), 2021

Akitoshi Ogawa1,2
1 Faculty of Medicine, Juntendo University, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, Japan
2 Brain Science Institute, Tamagawa University, Machida, Tokyo, Japan
Correspondence: Akitoshi Ogawa, Ph.D., Faculty of Medicine, Juntendo University, 2-1-1 Hongo, Bunkyo-ku, Tokyo, 113-8421, Japan. Email: a-ogawa@juntendo.ac.jp

Abstract: This study investigated whether the visual saliency in movies was associated with network centrality. Time-varying eigenvector centrality (EC) and participation coefficient (PC) were analyzed parcel-wise during movie-watching, retinotopy, and rest; time-varying EC in parietal parcels and time-varying PC in primary sensory parcels significantly correlated with visual saliency in the movies.

Functional images were downloaded from the HCP database. The movie-watching, retinotopy task, and resting-state (both 7T and 3T images) data of 168 participants (64 males and 104 females; 22–25 years: 19; 26–30 years: 82; 31–35 years: 65; ≥ 36 years: 2) were analyzed. 7T: TR, 1000 ms; TE, 22.2 ms; Flip Angle, 45 degrees; Field of View, 208 mm × 208 mm; Voxel size, 1.6 mm isotropic; 85 slices; Multiband factor, 5; Image acceleration factor, 2; Partial Fourier, 7/8; Echo spacing, 0.64 ms; Band-width, 1924 Hz/Px. 3T: TR, 720 ms; TE, 33.1 ms; Flip Angle, 52 degrees; Field of View, 208 mm × 180 mm; Voxel size, 2.0 mm isotropic; 72 slices; Multiband factor, 8; No image acceleration; Partial Fourier, 7/8; Echo spacing, 0.58 ms; Band-width, 2290 Hz/Px.

MOVIE: CC and Hollywood movies were presented (1024 × 768; 24 fps) with audio via earbuds. Run durations: 15 min 21 s (CC), 15 min 18 s (HO), 15 min 15 s (CC), 15 min 01 s (HO). Rest phases (20 s) at start and end of each run.
RET: Six fMRI runs with retinotopic stimuli (counter-clockwise/clockwise sweeps, expanding/contracting circles, two multi-direction bar sweeps) within 16° visual angle (1024 × 768; 15 fps). Each run lasted 5 min.

Image preprocessing: susceptibility-induced distortion correction; spatial normalization into MNI standard space; projection/normalization to standard surface (32,492 vertices/hemisphere); temporal high-pass filter (REST: 0.0005 Hz; MOVIE/RET: 0.005 Hz); FMRIB’s ICA-based Xnoiseifier (FIX); MSMAll multimodal surface matching. Preprocessed files are available from the HCP web page (db.humanconnectome.org, RRID:SCR_004830).

Network analyses: A proportional 7.5% threshold was applied to correlation matrices to generate binary undirected adjacency matrices, based on the peak of the mean flow coefficient across 2.5–15% proportions. Parcellation: HCP parcellation (180 parcels/hemisphere); parcel time-series averaged across vertices. Eigenvector centrality (EC) and participation coefficient (PC) were computed from these adjacency matrices.

Visual saliency: Saliency Toolbox v2.3 computed visual saliency maps (64×45) per movie frame using intensity, color, and orientation features with center–surround normalization. Mean visual saliency signal per scan was obtained by spatially and temporally averaging and then low-pass filtered at 0.1 Hz.

Parcel-wise relations: Temporal correlations were computed between the mean visual saliency signal and time-varying EC (tEC) and tPC (sliding window 50 s, computed every 1 s; excluding first/last 25 s). Correlation coefficients were Fisher-z transformed and Bonferroni-corrected; statistical threshold Z > 4.3 (P-FWE < 0.01).

Availability: Open access under Creative Commons Attribution License. The centrality maps and statistical results on the standard surface will be made available on reasonable request.

Figure 1A shows the procedure to calculate a centrality map on
the standard brain surface. The time-series of the preprocessed data
were averaged across vertices in each parcel. For this purpose, the HCP
parcellation, including 180 parcels in each hemisphere (Glasser et al.,
2016), was employed. The averaged time-series in each parcel for each
fMRI run was normalized to mean and standard deviation values of 0
and 1, respectively. The time-series were subsequently concatenated
across the fMRI runs of each participant for centrality analysis. A cor-
relation matrix was calculated for the concatenated time-series across
all parcels.

Figure 1A shows the procedure to calculate a centrality map on
the standard brain surface. The time-series of the preprocessed data
were averaged across vertices in each parcel. For this purpose, the HCP
parcellation, including 180 parcels in each hemisphere (Glasser et al.,
2016), was employed. The averaged time-series in each parcel for each
fMRI run was normalized to mean and standard deviation values of 0
and 1, respectively. The time-series were subsequently concatenated
across the fMRI runs of each participant for centrality analysis. A cor-
relation matrix was calculated for the concatenated time-series across
all parcels. Midnight Scan Club scripts (github.com/MidnightScanClub,
Gordon et al., 2017) were used to read and write CIFTI files. The HCP
ConnectomeWorkbench (Marcus et al., 2011, RRID:SCR_008750) was
used to calculate the correlation matrix and visualize the results.

A proportional 7.5% threshold was applied to the correlation matrix to
generate an adjacency matrix, which represented a binary undirected
network (van den Heuvel et al., 2017; Figure 1). The adjacency matrix
was used for calculating EC and PC. The threshold was determined
based on the flow coefficient (Honey et al., 2007). As opposed to EC
and PC, the flow coefficient is a local centrality metric. With respect to
the network construction, the network nodes are expected to influence
or communicate with each other more intensively. The mean flow coef-
ficients across participants were calculated at 2.5%, 5.0%, 7.5%, 10.0%,
12.5%, and 15% proportions. The peak was found at 7.5%.

EC evaluates the importance of each network node—parcel—
(Lohmann et al., 2010; Zuo et al., 2012). All connections in the adja-
cency matrix were used to calculate EC. Therefore, EC integrates the
connectivity information about all functionally connected parcels. EC
of parcel i was calculated as below:
ECi = 1 / λ1 A μ1 = 1 / λ1 Σ_j aij μ1(j).

PC of parcel i was also calculated for the brain network (Guimerà &
Nunes Amaral, 2005; Power et al., 2013):
PCi = 1 − Σ_m∈M (Ki(m) / Ki)^2.
M is the total set of network communities estimated using Louvain
community detection (Rubinov & Sporns, 2010), Ki is the number of
connections associated with parcel i, and Ki(m) is the number of con-
nections between parcel i and all parcels in community m. PC can be
used to define a parcel acting as a connector hub between modules
(i.e. local sub-networks) (Guimerà & Nunes Amaral, 2005; Rubinov &
Sporns, 2010; Bertolero et al., 2015; Cohen & D’Esposito, 2016).

Both time-varying eigenvector centrality (tEC) and participation
coefficient (tPC) were calculated using the sliding window technique
(Shakil et al., 2016). The window was set to 50 s (from before 25 s to
after 25 s). The tEC and the tPC were calculated every second in time
with the scan TR in MOVIE, except the first and the last 25 s. At time t,
the adjacency matrix A(t) was calculated. Then, the tEC of parcel i at
time t was calculated as below:
tECi(t) = 1 / λ1(t) A(t) μ1(t) = 1 / λ1(t) Σ_j aij(t) μ1(j,t).
The total set of network communities of time t, M(t), was estimated
from the adjacency matrix A(t). The tPC of parcel i was also calculated
as below:
tPCi(t) = 1 − Σ_m∈M(t) (Ki(m,t) / Ki(t))^2.

The brain connectivity toolbox (Rubinov & Sporns, 2010,
RRID:SCR_004841) was used to calculate flow coefficient, EC,
PC, tEC, and tPC.
